But I'm not sure how familiar people are with the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) or the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS). They're a little unique compared to other enforcement agencies due to their unique mandate. If BLM and FWS want you off a specific parcel of land, there's almost nothing you can do about it. Their mandate entirely federal in scope which overrides any state or local jurisdiction immediately, which means they have authorization from congress (like it or not) to do whatever they deem necessary to preserve or restore land in the U.S-- even if it means nearly outright taking it from someone. Desert and Arid ecosystems are particularly delicate due to the climate and BLM/FWS are quite unfriendly towards what they see as destructive practices (especially ranching, they really really don't like it..) when they deem an area in need of protection.

Their mandate is so incredibly specialized that pretty much whatever they say goes, almost without second thought. You and I don't have to like it, but that's literally how it is.

In Section A2,

(a2) During the 1970’s the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), in conjunction with the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), took a different approach to get the ranchers to sell. Ranchers were told that, “grazing was detrimental to wildlife and must be reduced”. 32 out of 53 permits were revoked and many ranchers were forced to leave. Grazing fees were raised significantly for those who were allowed to remain. Refuge personnel took over the irrigation system claiming it as their own.

They're legally allowed to do this. They can revoke permits at will, no questions asked-- as well as, raise grazing fees, and seize water resources. If they even feel in the tip of their little fingers that water resources are being diverted away from from a protected area somehow-- they can seize it immediately. This pretty much covers Sections A3, A4, B, and C.

Like I said, you and I don't have to like it, but in the eyes of the law-- BLM and FWS can do this. In section D, the Hammonds property had been split into chunks with the Refuge going in between the property. That entire cut off upper plot was pretty much a lost cause at that point. Once you have, now federal, land going through what remains of your property in a situation like this theres nothing you can do.

And in Section E,

(e) Shortly after the road & water disputes, the BLM & FWS arbitrarily revoked the Hammond’s upper grazing permit without any given cause, court proceeding or court ruling. As a traditional “fence out state” Oregon requires no obligation on the part of an owner to keep his or her livestock within a fence or to maintain control over the movement of the livestock. The Hammonds intended to still use their private property for grazing. However, they were informed that a federal judge ruled, in a federal court, that the federal government did not have to observe the Oregon fence out law. “Those laws are for the people, not for them”.

This is also entirely legal, due to the override of their federal mandate.

Sucks for the Hammonds of losing their livelihood, but if you're familiar with how BLM and FWS operate, starting in Section A2-- you would know that this was a lost cause and nothing but down hill for the private property owners. BLM and FWS are the agencies that you pretty much cannot fight, because legally, they're "un-fightable".

I'm not taking sides here, just stating the facts of how BLM/FWS operate for people that don't know what they can do.

It's natural to want a site like this to grow, but more doesn't mean better. We can't have a huge community AND a good community at the same time. Reddit learned this, 4chan learned this, Somethingawful learned this. Voat will probably sell out eventually, it's part of the life cycle of online communities which goes roughly like this:

1) Young college kids make a fun website in their free time that gathers a niche online following. The community is vibrant, but website isn't making money and as the site grows the bills increase. The college kids come up with clever ways to break even (donations, paid banners, etc) and since they are idealistic college kids keeping the community alive is all that matters.

2) The college kids who made the site graduate and enter the real world. They find out that working a 9-5 is not fun, but they have this growing online community that if they could just figure out a way to make profitable, would give them an out from the rat race. They try a bunch of different non-intrusive things to get the website profitable enough to quit their jobs, but they never quite get there.

3) They admit to each other that they need help from someone with experience. The kids meet with a business consultant or venture capitalist that finally "talks sense" into them. The VC offers a large infusion of cash that will let them actually pay themselves a salary, quit their jobs, and even get a fancy office. Of course there is an understanding that the VC wants a return on that investment.

4) The website founders start thinking about the website as a financial asset and not a fun side project. They change the TOS, start making behind the scenes deals with advertisers, start kicking out users and moderators that they don't think contribute to the population growth. The website starts to become sanitized and to the casual user it seems like a good thing as the 'bullies' are removed. But to the older members of the community they long for the way things used to be. So a fragment of the old user base breaks off and goes to a different website (Somethingawful -> 4chan -> Various chans or Digg -> Reddit -> Voat).

It may not happen to Voat exactly like what I just described. But the reality is that Atko is going to graduate college, he's going to lose his idealism, he is going to feel the same financial pressure we all feel, and eventually he's going to have the same type business meetings that the guys from reddit had. I just hope it happens later than sooner.
